explanations.explanation: Kindness it is, baker. David, Israel's king, says, “I will show kindness to Hanun son of Nahash, just as his father showed kindness to me.” Hanun is the new king of the Ammonites, and David wants to pay back a favor. Most of us can't even return a borrowed ladder, and David is repaying a whole kingdom's worth of kindness.

I get why strength comes to mind, friend, because this chapter has armies all over it. But at this point David isn't flexing anything. The text says David will show kindness to Hanun, just as Hanun's father showed kindness to him. The strength shows up later, once the trouble starts.

Justice sounds like a serious word, and it doesn't fit here. David isn't settling a score with Hanun. The text says he will show kindness, because Hanun's father showed kindness to him. Think of a thank-you note instead of a courtroom.

True, baker. The text says David sent some of his servants to console Hanun concerning his father. That's a sympathy visit, the kind where you show up and say, "I'm so sorry for your loss." David meant it as comfort, and that's the whole plan.

Not this time, friend. The text says David did send some of his servants to console Hanun concerning his father. Hanun is the new Ammonite king, and his father has just died. So this is a visit meant as comfort, and David sends his own servants to deliver it.

explanations.answer: Spy out the city and overthrow it
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The princes ask Hanun, “Has not David instead sent his servants to explore the city, spy it out, and overthrow it?” Notice they ask it as a question, with David's kind visit sitting right there. They're saying the comforters are scouts.

No treasury talk in this passage, friend. The princes never mention stealing anything. They say David sent his servants “to explore the city, spy it out, and overthrow it.” That's a much bigger accusation than sticky fingers.

explanations.answer: Take Hanun back as a prisoner
explanations.explanation: That's a dramatic idea, but the princes don't say it. They never talk about Hanun being taken anywhere. Their accusation is about the city: the servants came to explore it, spy it out, and overthrow it.
Half, baker. The text says Hanun shaved off half of each man's beard. I think this one hurts, so I'll say it plainly. David's servants came to comfort and were treated this way instead.

That would be a clean sweep, friend, but the text says half. Hanun shaved off half of each man's beard. I think a half-job like that is made to be noticed. Whatever the reason, it's what the text says.

Close on the fractions, baker, but this one is a different number. The text says Hanun shaved off half of each man's beard. These are David's servants, who came to console him. I think this part stings, so I won't make it a joke.

Right, baker. David tells them, “Stay in Jericho until your beards have grown back, and then return.” Before that, he sends messengers to meet them. That's a king looking after his men. And a beard has its own timer, one that nobody can speed up.

An apology would be nice, friend, but the text never mentions one. David's instruction is “Stay in Jericho until your beards have grown back, and then return.” He sends messengers to meet the men, since they had been thoroughly humiliated. His instruction is about the beards, with no apology involved.

David's army does move later in the passage, baker, but that isn't his instruction here. He says, “Stay in Jericho until your beards have grown back, and then return.” The men aren't waiting on an army. They're waiting on their beards.

Not quite, friend. Look at what the text says they do. The Ammonites hire twenty thousand Aramean foot soldiers, a thousand men from the king of Maacah and twelve thousand men from Tob. No gift basket in sight. They're getting ready for a fight.

False is right, baker. When the Ammonites realized they had become a stench to David, they hired soldiers. They didn't send a gift. Their answer to David's anger was to bring in an army, and that's all the text tells us.

explanations.answer: Sends out the entire army of mighty men
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The text says, “David sent Joab and the entire army of mighty men.” Joab is David's commander (2 Samuel 8:16). The Ammonites hired a crowd, and David answered with his whole army of mighty men.

explanations.answer: Sends his servants back to make peace with Hanun
explanations.explanation: David already tried sending servants, and we saw how that visit went. This time the text says he sent Joab and the entire army of mighty men. Friend, nobody's carrying a sympathy card on this trip.

explanations.answer: Goes alone to talk things over with Hanun
explanations.explanation: A solo sit-down sounds peaceful, baker, but that's not what happens. The text says David sent Joab and the entire army of mighty men. No lone visit, and no small group either. The whole army goes.

Yes, baker. Joab picks some of Israel's best men to face the Arameans, then puts the rest under his brother Abishai to face the Ammonites. One army, two fronts, no panic. Joab saw trouble ahead and behind and made a plan.

Going home might feel tempting with lines in front and behind, friend. But the text shows Joab doing the opposite. He sets up two groups, one against the Arameans and one under Abishai against the Ammonites. Nobody's heading home yet.

Joab doesn't wait, baker. David isn't on the field here. He sends Joab and the army, and Joab takes charge himself. David only goes out personally later, when he crosses the Jordan to Helam (2 Samuel 10:17).

Best, baker. The text says Joab “selected some of the best men of Israel” and lined them up against the Arameans. That makes sense to me. The Arameans are the group that came in from outside, so he sends his strongest group at them.
Newest isn't the word, friend. The text says Joab selected some of the best men of Israel for the Arameans. He picks them for how good they are at fighting. Everyone else goes under Abishai.
Not oldest, baker. Joab's pick is “some of the best men of Israel,” and he lines them up against the Arameans. The text doesn't mention anyone's age. What it gives is the word best.

explanations.answer: If one of them is overpowered the other comes to help
explanations.explanation: That's the plan, baker. Joab tells Abishai, “then you will come to my rescue. And if the Ammonites are too strong for you, then I will come to your rescue.” It's like two friends texting, "Just yell if you need me." Each brother is covering the other.

explanations.answer: If one of them wins first he chases the enemy home
explanations.explanation: Chasing is not what Joab plans, friend. What he says is about rescue: if the Arameans are too strong for him, Abishai comes. If the Ammonites are too strong for Abishai, Joab comes. They're watching each other's backs.

explanations.answer: If one of them is overpowered they both retreat
explanations.explanation: Retreat isn't in the plan, baker. Joab says, “then you will come to my rescue. And if the Ammonites are too strong for you, then I will come to your rescue.” It's a plan to help each other, with no backing out. Brothers, side by side.

True, baker. Joab says, “Be strong and let us fight bravely for our people and for the cities of our God.” He's speaking to his brother, with the army listening. That's a pep talk with real stakes behind it.

It's actually true, friend. Joab says, “Be strong and let us fight bravely for our people and for the cities of our God.” Those words come right after he tells Abishai how they'll rescue each other. It's a pep talk before the battle starts.
Not so, baker. When Joab and his troops advance, the Arameans “fled before him.” They never stand and fight. That's one very short battle for a very big hiring bill.
False is correct, baker. Joab and his troops advance to fight the Arameans, and the Arameans fled before him. That's quick. Then the Ammonites see it and run too (2 Samuel 10:14).

Shobach, baker. He's the commander of Hadadezer's army, and he leads the new Aramean troops to Helam. Hadadezer, king of Zobah (2 Samuel 8:3), is the one who sent for them. Keep that name, because Shobach's story ends there.
Abner is a real name in the Bible, friend, but not in this passage. He's Saul's army commander (1 Samuel 14:50). The commander leading the Arameans to Helam is Shobach. He leads Hadadezer's army.

Sisera is a commander, baker, but he's from another story. The Bible calls him the commander of Jabin's army (Judges 4:2). Here the commander of Hadadezer's army, leading the Arameans to Helam, is Shobach.
Not this time, baker. David doesn't stay home and send Joab again. The text says he gathered all Israel, crossed the Jordan, and went to Helam. The king goes himself.
False, baker. When the report reaches David, “he gathered all Israel, crossed the Jordan, and went to Helam.” He doesn't stay in Jerusalem. The Arameans then line up against David himself.

Yes, baker. The text says the Arameans “fled before Israel.” The text even tells us David killed seven hundred charioteers and forty thousand foot soldiers, and struck down Shobach. It's a heavy part, so I'll leave it at that.

Surrounding David's army would be a big move, friend, but it's not what the text shows. The Arameans arrayed themselves against David and fought, then fled before Israel. So the result goes the other way.

explanations.answer: They push Israel back across the Jordan
explanations.explanation: David crosses the Jordan to get to Helam, baker, and he stays there. The Arameans don't push anybody back. The text says they “fled before Israel.”

explanations.answer: Make peace and become subject to Israel
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The text says that when all the kings subject to Hadadezer saw they had been defeated by Israel, they “made peace with Israel and became subject to them.” Those are the kings who had stood behind Hadadezer. They end up making peace with Israel.

explanations.answer: Hire another army from Tob and Maacah
explanations.explanation: Hiring was the Ammonites' move earlier, friend. The men of Tob and Maacah were already part of that crowd. After Helam, these kings make peace with Israel and become subject to them.

explanations.answer: Hide inside the Ammonite city with Hanun
explanations.explanation: The Ammonites went into their city earlier in the passage, baker, but these kings don't join them. The text says they made peace with Israel and became subject to them. Hanun's city doesn't come up for them at all.

Not anymore, baker. The last line of the passage says, “So the Arameans were afraid to help the Ammonites anymore.” The Ammonites hired a crowd, and in the end the help was gone. The story closes with the Arameans out of the picture.
False, baker. The text says, “So the Arameans were afraid to help the Ammonites anymore.” The kings had made peace with Israel by then. The Ammonites were left without those helpers.
